prompt: When a quick look isn't enough, how can you decide whether two protons in a molecule are equivalent?

choices.text: Compare the structures that would form if each hydrogen in turn were replaced by an X group
Check whether they are bonded to the same carbon
choices.why: Protons on the same carbon can be nonequivalent (diastereotopic), and protons on different carbons can be equivalent.

choices.text: Count how many neighboring protons each one has
choices.why: Neighbors decide splitting, not equivalence. The test is to replace each H by X and compare the products.

choices.text: Check whether both are bonded to sp3 carbons
choices.why: Many protons on sp3 carbons are nonequivalent, like the –CH3 and –CH2– protons of butane.

explanation: The equivalence or nonequivalence of two protons can be determined by comparing the structures that would be formed if each hydrogen were replaced by an X group. The products can be constitutional isomers, identical, enantiomers or diastereomers.

prompt: Replacing any one of the six –CH3 hydrogens of butane with X gives the identical product. What are these hydrogens called?

choices.why: Enantiotopic hydrogens give enantiomers when replaced, not the identical product.
Diastereotopic hydrogens give diastereomers when replaced.
Unrelated hydrogens give constitutional isomers when replaced.

explanation: Hydrogens that give the same product whichever one is replaced by X are chemically identical and are called homotopic. The six –CH3 hydrogens on carbons 1 and 4 of butane are homotopic and show an identical NMR absorption.

prompt: In butane, how is a –CH3 hydrogen related to a –CH2– hydrogen?

choices.text: They are chemically unrelated: replacing them by X gives constitutional isomers
They are homotopic: replacing them by X gives the same product
choices.why: Replacing a –CH3 hydrogen gives a 1-substituted butane, and replacing a –CH2– hydrogen gives a 2-substituted butane; those are different compounds.

choices.text: They are enantiotopic: replacing them by X gives enantiomers
choices.why: The two products differ in where X is attached, so they are constitutional isomers, not enantiomers.

choices.text: They are diastereotopic: replacing them by X gives diastereomers
choices.why: The two products have different connections, so they are constitutional isomers.

explanation: In butane, the –CH3 protons are different from the –CH2– protons. Substitution by X gives different constitutional isomers, so the protons are chemically unrelated and would likely show different NMR absorptions.

prompt: What are the two hydrogens on carbon 2 of butane called?

choices.text: Enantiotopic, because replacing one or the other by X gives enantiomers
Homotopic, because replacing either by X gives the same product
choices.why: Replacing either one makes carbon 2 a new chirality center, so the two products are enantiomers, not identical.

choices.text: Diastereotopic, because replacing either by X gives diastereomers
choices.why: Butane has no chirality center to begin with, so only one forms, and the products are enantiomers.

choices.text: Unrelated, because replacing them by X gives constitutional isomers
choices.why: Both hydrogens are on carbon 2, so the products have the same connections.

explanation: Substituting X for a hydrogen on carbon 2 of butane forms a new chirality center. Replacing the pro-R or the pro-S hydrogen gives different enantiomers, so the two hydrogens are enantiotopic.

prompt: Do enantiotopic hydrogens give the same NMR absorption?

choices.text: Yes; though not identical, they are electronically equivalent
No; because they aren't identical, they absorb at different positions
choices.why: Enantiotopic hydrogens are not identical, but they are electronically equivalent and show the same absorption.
In a chiral molecule such as (R)-2-butanol, the comparable hydrogens are diastereotopic and likely absorb differently.

choices.text: Only on a spectrometer of 500 MHz or more
choices.why: Equivalence doesn't depend on the instrument. Enantiotopic hydrogens absorb together on any spectrometer.

explanation: Enantiotopic hydrogens, even though not identical, are nevertheless electronically equivalent and thus have the same NMR absorption.

prompt: Two hydrogens in a molecule are diastereotopic. What does that mean?

choices.text: Replacing one or the other by X gives diastereomers, and they likely absorb at different positions
Replacing one or the other by X gives diastereomers, but they absorb at the same position
choices.why: Diastereotopic hydrogens are neither chemically nor electronically equivalent, so they likely show different absorptions.

choices.text: Replacing one or the other by X gives enantiomers, and they absorb at the same position
choices.why: That describes enantiotopic hydrogens.

choices.text: Replacing one or the other by X gives the same product
choices.why: That describes homotopic hydrogens.

explanation: Hydrogens whose substitution by X leads to different diastereomers are diastereotopic. They are neither chemically nor electronically equivalent and would likely show different NMR absorptions.

prompt: How are the two –CH2– hydrogens on carbon 3 of (R)-2-butanol, CH3CH(OH)CH2CH3, related?

choices.why: (R)-2-Butanol already has a chirality center. Replacing either hydrogen forms a second one, so the products are diastereomers, not enantiomers.
Replacing one or the other hydrogen gives two different products, not the same one.
Both hydrogens are on carbon 3, so the products have the same connections.

explanation: Because substitution of a hydrogen at carbon 3 of the chiral (R)-2-butanol forms a second chirality center, replacing the pro-R or pro-S hydrogen gives different diastereomers. The two hydrogens are diastereotopic.

prompt: How are the two –CH2– hydrogens on carbon 4 of 2-methyl-3-pentanone, (CH3)2CHCOCH2CH3, related?

choices.why: The molecule has no chirality center, so replacing either hydrogen makes only one, and the products are enantiomers.
Replacing either hydrogen makes carbon 4 a chirality center, so the two products are enantiomers, not the same compound.
Both hydrogens are on carbon 4, so the products have the same connections.

explanation: 2-Methyl-3-pentanone is achiral. Replacing either hydrogen on carbon 4 by X creates a single new chirality center, so the two possible products are enantiomers and the hydrogens are enantiotopic (Exercise 13.7.1).

prompt: How are the two hydrogens on carbon 3 of cyclohexanol related?

choices.why: Replacing either hydrogen by X makes both carbon 1 and carbon 3 chirality centers, so the products are diastereomers (X cis or trans to OH), not enantiomers.
One replacement puts X on the same side of the ring as the OH and the other puts it on the opposite side, giving two different compounds.
Both hydrogens are on carbon 3, so the products have the same connections.

explanation: Replacing one hydrogen on carbon 3 of cyclohexanol by X gives the product with X cis to the OH; replacing the other gives X trans to the OH. These products are diastereomers, so the hydrogens are diastereotopic (Exercise 13.7.1).

prompt: cis-Bicyclo[3.3.0]octane is two cyclopentane rings sharing one C–C bond, with both ring-fusion hydrogens on the same face. How are those two ring-fusion hydrogens related?

choices.why: Replacing either ring-fusion hydrogen gives the identical compound, not a pair of enantiomers.
Replacing either ring-fusion hydrogen gives the identical compound, not a pair of diastereomers.
The two ring-fusion positions are alike, so the products aren't constitutional isomers.

explanation: The molecule is symmetrical, so replacing either ring-fusion hydrogen by X gives the same product. The two hydrogens are homotopic (Exercise 13.7.1).

prompt: How many kinds of electronically nonequivalent protons does CH3OCH2CH(CH3)2 have?
explanation: The kinds are CH3O–, –OCH2–, –CH– and the two equivalent methyls of (CH3)2CH–. That gives four kinds, so up to four NMR absorptions (Exercise 13.7.2).

prompt: How many kinds of electronically nonequivalent protons does CH3CH2CH2NO2 have?
explanation: The –CH3, the middle –CH2– and the –CH2NO2 protons are three different kinds (Exercise 13.7.2).

prompt: How many kinds of electronically nonequivalent protons does methylbenzene (toluene), C6H5CH3, have?
explanation: The methyl protons are one kind. The ring protons ortho, meta and para to the methyl group are three more kinds, for four in all (Exercise 13.7.2).

prompt: How many kinds of electronically nonequivalent protons does 2-methyl-1-butene, CH2=C(CH3)CH2CH3, have?
explanation: The two =CH2 protons are nonequivalent (one is cis to the methyl and one cis to the ethyl group). Add the methyl on carbon 2, the –CH2– and the –CH3 of the ethyl group: five kinds (Exercise 13.7.2).

prompt: How many absorptions would you expect in the ^1H NMR spectrum of (S)-malate, ^−O2CCH(OH)CH2CO2^−, counting the OH proton?
explanation: Malate is chiral, so the two –CH2– protons next to the chirality center are diastereotopic and give separate absorptions. With the –CH(OH)– proton and the OH proton, that makes four (Exercise 13.7.3).
